questions.q: How many physical qubits does a distance-11 surface code need to protect 1 logical qubit?
questions.explain: Using total = 2d^2-1 with d=11: 2(121)-1 = 241, matching the verified table.

questions.q: How does physical-qubit cost scale with concatenation level L for the Steane code family?
options: As L^7 -- polynomially of high degree
It stays constant at 7 qubits regardless of L
questions.explain: Each concatenation level multiplies the physical-qubit count by 7, giving 7^L total -- exponential growth, verified directly for L=1 through 4 (7, 49, 343, 2401).

questions.q: At concatenation level 1, the Steane code uses only 7 qubits -- fewer than even a distance-3 surface code's 17. Why doesn't this make concatenation the better choice overall?
options: Concatenation's cost grows exponentially with level, while the surface code's grows only quadratically with distance, so concatenation becomes far more expensive at the scales real algorithms need
The level-1 Steane code actually provides no error correction at all
17 qubits is actually cheaper than 7 qubits once more precise accounting is used
The comparison between concatenation levels and surface-code distances is entirely meaningless
questions.explain: The lesson's honest point is that a cheaper-looking small-scale number can be misleading -- exponential growth (concatenation) always eventually overtakes quadratic growth (surface code) as more protection is needed.

questions.q: By concatenation level 4, how many physical qubits does the Steane-style concatenated code require, and how does that compare to a distance-15 surface code's cost?
options: 2,401 qubits at level 4, versus 449 qubits for a distance-15 surface code -- concatenation costs far more
2,401 qubits at level 4, versus 4,900 qubits for distance-15 -- concatenation is cheaper
343 qubits at level 4, identical to the distance-15 surface code
Level 4 concatenation requires fewer qubits than level 1
questions.explain: 7^4 = 2,401 physical qubits for level-4 concatenation versus 2(15^2)-1 = 449 for a distance-15 surface code -- a clear illustration of exponential growth overtaking quadratic growth.

questions.q: What is the central, honest point this lesson makes about comparing the surface code and concatenated codes?
options: The shape of the cost curve (quadratic vs exponential) matters more than which code looks cheaper at the smallest possible instance
Concatenated codes are always cheaper than the surface code at every scale
The surface code is cheap in an absolute sense, requiring very few physical qubits overall
Cost comparisons between code families are impossible to make meaningfully
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that looking only at the cheapest instance of each code family is misleading -- the growth rate (quadratic vs exponential) determines which approach is actually more practical at the scale real algorithms need.
